newsitem.title: USA: TRAFFIC, BUDGETS CONCERN U.S. STORM FORECASTERS.
newsitem.headline: TRAFFIC, BUDGETS CONCERN U.S. STORM FORECASTERS.

text.p: Lingering concerns about federal budget cuts and the possible loss of thousands of lives in traffic during evacuations were on the minds of storm forecasters on Thursday as they prepared for the 1997 Atlantic hurricane season, which starts June 1.

"The threat along the coast is increasing," Jerry Jarrell, deputy director of the National Hurricane Center, told a news conference at which the National Weather Service rolled out a new $41 million forecasting jet.

The number of people living in coastal areas at high risk from hurricane winds and flooding has mushroomed in recent years, making it likely that massive traffic jams would result if forecasters ordered an evacuation. Cars and trucks offer little shelter in the face of high winds and inches of rain brought by a powerful hurricane, the forecasters noted.

"There is a risk of a major disaster because of traffic. You are going to get a failed evacuation ... you will have hundreds or perhaps thousands of cars on the highway when a hurricane hits," Jarrell said. "We could lose literally hundreds of lives, and I only say hundreds because I shudder to think of losing thousands."

There was a 17-mile (27 km) traffic jam outside the Hampton Roads Bridge Tunnel near Norfolk, Virginia, in 1985 before Hurricane Gloria passed east of the city. And an estimated 10,000 people were on roadways around Pensacola, Florida, in 1994 when Hurricane Opal came ashore.

Opal, which had been one of the strongest ever, veered and collapsed just before reaching the coast, keeping the worst of its winds away from the traffic snafu. Forecasters had not counted on road construction that left highways unable to move the thousands of cars quickly.
"The potential for disaster is everywhere that we evacuate people," Jarrell said.

The National Oceanographic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) will begin using a new $41 million high-altitude Gulfstream-IV jet this year to fly high in the area around storms while they are still out at sea and obtain hitherto unavailable data about the air currents that steer them.
"Hopefully, this information is going to make a dramatic improvement in our forecasts," NOAA Administrator Jim Baker said.

For example, in August 1992, forecasters had expected Hurricane Andrew, which eventually came ashore south of Miami and caused more than $25 billion in damage, to make landfall well north of the city. The additional data available from the new jet could make such a storm's direction apparent earlier.

NOAA's fiscal 1997 budget includes enough money for about 93 hours of operation, about 10 flights, by the new jet, meaning forecasters could face difficult decisions about when to use it. It is expected to be used only for storms threatening the U.S. coastline and U.S. Caribbean islands.
Fiscal year 1998, which begins Oct. 1, has funding for about 135 hours, Naomi Surgi, the jet's mission manager at the National Hurricane Center, said.

The six-month Atlantic hurricane season ends on Nov. 30. An average season sees nine tropical storms, of which five or six grow to hurricane strength, and forecasters have predicted that this year will be busier than average.

The cost of flying the jet, estimated at more than $2,700 per hour, is not the only budget issue dogging hurricane forecasters, who dodged a bullet when Congress's new budget cut six members of the center's staff.

Money was found to avoid staff cuts for now but NOAA faces another budget battle at the end of the season. It needs about $10.8 million to fill positions that have been left empty and to perform maintenance and other functions, Baker said.
"We are facing some serious issues of temporary reductions," he said.
